newsitem.title: USA: Leftist Mexican candidate sees fairly clean vote.
newsitem.headline: Leftist Mexican candidate sees fairly clean vote.

text.p: Mexico City's leftist candidate for governor, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, said on Tuesday that the high political cost of committing egregious fraud in coming elections would prevent the government from doing so.

Running a fraudulent election would shake investor confidence in the stability of the country, too high a cost for the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party to risk, Cardenas said at a discussion held by the Americas Society here.

"The government will pay a high cost to commit fraud (like it did) in 1988," said Cardenas, who has twice run unsuccessfully as the presidential candidate of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

In the 1988 presidential race, official computers crashed when early returns showed Cardenas leading. When the count resumed, the PRI's Carlos Salinas de Gortari was ahead and was eventually declared the winner. The PRI denied cheating.
Recent opinion polls showed Cardenas leading the candidates of the PRI and of the conservative National Action Party (PAN) in the July 6 Mexico City race.
Voters will elect, for the first time, the governor of the Federal District of Mexico City, along with six state governors, and members of the lower house and half of the senate.

Although Cardenas said he does not expect egregious fraud, he said the election is far from fair in terms of resources available to candidates, with the PRI putting government support behind its candidates.
Outlining his platform, Cardenas emphasized his commitment to fighting corruption and to reallocating resources to housing and social services without raising taxes.
Foreign investment is important to the city and country, and privatization, except in "strategic sectors," should continue, he said.
"We don't make an ideological issue of privatization. It is an economic decision."

On the North American Free Trade Agreement, Cardenas said a compensatory fund for Mexico should have been included in the pact, similar to the arrangement for Spain and Portugal to join the European Union. At present, specific issues that affect Mexican tomato farmers and truckers should be resolved to make the agreement work, he said.
Cardenas said the July election is an important test that the reformed electoral system really works.

But he downplayed the speculation that the victory in this year's election would put him on the road to winning the presidency in 2000, saying that the performance of the winner over the next threee years would be crucial.
"Nobody should be thinking that winning this election (would make him) the candidate for 2000," he said.
